note:
THE 1832 TOWER IS THE LIGHT STANDING ON 1835-07-01, and this page gives its height, its builder and the story of its predecessor's collapse. Verbatim: "On March 3, 1831, Congress appropriated $5,000 for a lighthouse to mark the mouth of the Chicago River. According to History of Chicago by Alfred Theodore Andreas, Samuel Jackson was hired as the contractor, but before the lighthouse was completed, it collapsed on October 30, 1831. 'A few hours before it toppled over,' Andreas wrote, 'so confident were many there was no danger of its falling, that several went upon the top of it, some of the visitors being women. The walls were three feet thick, and the tower had been raised to a height of fifty feet.'" Then: "Jackson claimed the tower had been built on quicksand, which caused the tower to settle unevenly and fall, but others believed it was shoddy workmanship. Regardless, Jackson soon started work on a second tower and completed it the following year. This lighthouse stood forty feet high and employed four, fourteen-inch reflectors in its bird-cage lantern room. Samuel Lasby was employed as keeper of the light, which was the first established on Lake Michigan."

READ THE TWO TOWERS APART, BECAUSE THE ONLY FABRIC DETAIL ON THE PAGE BELONGS TO THE ONE THAT FELL. "The walls were three feet thick" and "a height of fifty feet" describe the FIRST tower, at the moment it collapsed, unfinished. The SECOND tower - the one standing in 1835 - gets exactly three attributes here: forty feet high, four fourteen-inch reflectors, a bird-cage lantern room. THE PAGE DOES NOT SAY THE 1832 TOWER WAS CONICAL, AND DOES NOT SAY WHAT IT WAS BUILT OF. docs/research/04-structures-south.md line 77 reads "forty feet high; conical stone/masonry" as [DOC] from Andreas, drloihjournal and lighthousefriends jointly, and data/exclusions.json calls it "the 1832 conical masonry tower" on andreas_1884_v1. Whatever supports "conical" and "masonry", it is not this page. Cite this page for the height, the builder, the date and the keeper; cite something else for the shape and the material, or mark them inferred.

NAME PRECISION: the contractor is "Samuel Jackson" here, not the "Mr. Jackson" of the brief. The first keeper is "Samuel Lasby"; chicagology_prefire052, quoting Chicago Magazine of March 1857, spells him "Samuel C. Lasby".

The page is a modern enthusiast synthesis with a stated bibliography, not a scholarly edition and not a period document. Tier 4 is the closest rung in this project's vocabulary for a modern textual compilation (tiers 5 and 6 are reserved for pictorial and cartographic material); it should not be read as "scholarly". Its 1830s content is a paraphrase of Andreas with two direct quotations, so it adds no independent witness to andreas_1884_v1 - it is a convenient, checkable restatement, and where a claim is load-bearing the volume is the thing to read.
